summary: The first half regulates when priests and members of their households may eat holy offerings, including temporary uncleanness, household status, and repayment after accidental eating. The second half addresses Israel and resident foreigners about acceptable sacrificial animals, newborn animals, thanksgiving offerings, and honoring Yahweh's holy name.
whyItMatters: The chapter protects holy food and altar gifts through boundaries of person, time, and condition, while showing that ritual uncleanness is temporary and that eligibility rules reflect an ancient priestly household system.

context.author: Leviticus presents Yahweh speaking these rules to Moses; the finished book does not name its narrator, and its composition history remains debated.
context.audience: Aaron and his sons receive the holy-food rules; Aaron, Israel, and resident foreigners receive the offering rules.
context.date: The laws are narrated at Sinai around the Tent of Meeting; the date of the book's received literary form is debated.
context.setting: Priestly households and the sanctuary, where holy portions are eaten and animals are presented at the altar.
context.literaryForm: Priestly access law followed by offering-quality rules and a closing appeal to the exodus and Yahweh's holy name.

outline.heading: Temporary uncleanness and holy food
outline.note: Priests may not eat holy food while unclean; for the contact case described, bathing and sunset mark the return to clean status.

outline.heading: Who belongs at the priestly table
outline.note: Household membership governs eating, while accidental consumption requires restoration plus one fifth.

outline.heading: Animals accepted for vows and freewill offerings
outline.note: Israelites and foreigners must bring animals meeting the stated requirements, with one limited exception for a freewill gift.

outline.heading: Newborn animals and thanksgiving
outline.note: An animal remains with its mother seven days, mother and young are not killed on one day, and thanksgiving meat is eaten the day offered.

outline.heading: The holy name and the exodus
outline.note: The conclusion grounds obedience and sanctification in Yahweh bringing Israel out of Egypt.

keyVerses.text: When the sun is down, he shall be clean; and afterward he shall eat of the holy things, because it is his bread.
keyVerses.why: Sunset restores holy-food access in the preceding contact-purity case.

keyVerses.text: “‘If a man eats something holy unwittingly, then he shall add the fifth part of its value to it, and shall give the holy thing to the priest.
keyVerses.why: Accidental eating requires restitution with an added fifth.

keyVerses.text: You shall not profane my holy name, but I will be made holy among the children of Israel. I am Yahweh who makes you holy,
keyVerses.why: The chapter connects protection of holy things with God’s name and sanctification.

themes: limits involving animal mothers and young

questions.question: Does a priest's uncleanness permanently remove him from holy food?
questions.answer: No. The ban lasts only while the priest remains unclean. For the contact case in verses 5-7, bathing and sunset restore clean status; verse 4 names other conditions without restating their complete purification procedures. Ritual uncleanness is not a verdict that he is morally corrupt or permanently excluded.

questions.question: What sources of uncleanness are named?
questions.answer: The chapter lists a skin condition, a discharge, contact with death, seminal emission, contact with a creeping thing, contact with another unclean person, and eating an animal that died or was torn. The list governs holy-food access rather than diagnosing moral character.

questions.question: Who may eat from a priest's holy food?
questions.answer: A foreigner living with a priest and a hired servant may not eat the holy portions. A person the priest has bought as a slave and those born in the household may eat, and a childless widowed or divorced daughter may return to the table after returning home. Household membership governs access, including the unequal status of people owned as slaves.

questions.question: What is a heave offering in the priest's household rules?
questions.answer: Verse 12 names it as one category of holy food from which a priest's daughter is excluded when she marries an outsider. The chapter assumes the offering system already described and focuses here on eligibility to eat rather than the presentation movement.

questions.question: What happens if someone eats holy food by mistake?
questions.answer: The person must restore what was eaten to the priest and add one fifth of its value. The following warning makes priests responsible for guarding the holy things so that eating them does not bring guilt on the people.

questions.question: Which animals are excluded, including gifts received from foreigners?
questions.answer: The law rejects animals that are blind, injured, maimed, affected by the listed sores, or have damaged testicles. The same exclusion applies if the animal comes from a foreigner; changing the donor does not change its acceptability. Verse 23 separately permits specified bodily irregularities for a freewill gift but not for fulfilling a vow.

questions.question: Why may a deformed animal be a freewill offering but not fulfill a vow?
questions.answer: Verse 23 makes that narrow distinction for a bull or lamb while keeping the broader no-defect rule for required acceptance. The chapter states the exception but does not explain why a freewill gift and fulfillment of a vow are evaluated differently.

questions.question: What protections involving animal mothers and young appear?
questions.answer: A newborn bull, sheep, or goat remains with its mother for seven days before becoming eligible, and a cow or ewe may not be killed on the same day as its young. The text sets those limits without presenting a complete theory of animal welfare.

questions.question: How does the exodus ground the closing commands?
questions.answer: Yahweh identifies himself as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt to be their God and who makes them holy. The chapter therefore places careful treatment of holy food and offerings within a relationship begun by liberation, not merely within technical rule keeping.

glossary.def: Offerings dedicated by Israel to Yahweh, portions of which become the priests' protected food.
A temporary ritual status that suspends access to holy food until the stated cleansing and waiting are complete.
A dedicated offering portion; here the term appears while defining a priest's daughter's right to eat.
A voluntarily brought offering distinguished here from one presented to fulfill a vow.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The preceding chapter limits priestly mourning, marriage, and altar service, while allowing priests with listed bodily conditions to eat holy food. This chapter explains when eating that food is itself restricted.

here.text: Ritual status and household membership govern holy-food access. Rules for animal quality, newborn animals, and thanksgiving offerings then broaden the address to Israel and resident foreigners.

after.text: The next chapter organizes Sabbath and annual observances by appointed times, offerings, assemblies, rest, harvest sharing, and the memory of leaving Egypt.
